name: Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud
title: Phantom Vendors and Procurement Fraud
answer: Phantom vendors are supplier records that exist only on paper or in a system, created to route payments to a fraudster rather than a real provider of goods or services. Procurement fraud of this kind also includes shell companies, inflated invoices, duplicate payments, and collusion between employees and outside parties. AI work in this area focuses on finding vendor identities, payment patterns, and purchasing behaviours that are statistically unusual or structurally inconsistent with legitimate trade. The scope covers both detection after the fact and early warning during invoice approval and vendor onboarding.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Phantom vendors are supplier records that exist only on paper or in a system, created to route payments to a fraudster rather than a real provider of goods or services. Procurement fraud of this kind also includes shell companies, inflated invoices, duplicate payments, and collusion between employees and outside parties. AI work in this area focuses on finding vendor identities, payment patterns, and purchasing behaviours that are statistically unusual or structurally inconsistent with legitimate trade. The scope covers both detection after the fact and early warning during invoice approval and vendor onboarding.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: This work runs on the ordinary systems of a finance function: enterprise resource planning platforms, accounts payable ledgers, procurement databases, contract repositories, and corporate email or document stores. AI models are typically deployed as a layer over these systems, ingesting vendor master files, invoice line items, payment runs, and employee records. Cloud analytics environments and secure data warehouses are common because they allow the model to join records across departments without disturbing live transaction processing. Access controls and audit logs are essential, since the underlying data includes bank details, tax identifiers, and personal information about staff and suppliers.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by combining rules-based checks with machine learning models that learn normal purchasing behaviour for each business unit, category, and vendor. Entity resolution links vendor records that share addresses, bank accounts, phone numbers, or beneficial owners, which often exposes shell companies and duplicate suppliers. Anomaly detection flags invoices that arrive just under approval thresholds, payments to newly created vendors, or purchases with no matching delivery receipt. Network analysis then maps relationships among employees, approvers, and vendors to reveal conflicts of interest or circular payment flows.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on the fact that these models process sensitive personal data and can implicate employees or suppliers before any finding is proven. False positives can delay legitimate payments, damage supplier relationships, or trigger internal investigations that harm reputations, so human review and clear escalation rules are standard practice. Provenance matters because a model's output is only as defensible as the source records behind it, and investigators need to trace every flag back to the original invoice, purchase order, or vendor change request. Organisations must also respect employment law, data protection rules, and contractual confidentiality when monitoring staff communications or sharing findings with law enforcement.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous monitoring rather than periodic audits, with models scoring every vendor and invoice as they arrive instead of sampling past transactions. Generative AI is beginning to help investigators summarise vendor histories, draft interview questions, and explain why a particular supplier looks suspicious. Future systems are likely to combine external data on company registries, sanctions lists, and beneficial ownership with internal records, making it harder for phantom vendors to hide behind fragmented information. The goal is not to replace forensic accountants but to give them a much shorter list of high-risk cases to examine.
